definition: Fluctuate means to rise and fall irregularly.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fluctuate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fluctuate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Tips at the diner fluctuate wildly — a rainy Tuesday can bring in twice what a sunny one does, and nobody has ever worked out why.
Drift is milder than fluctuate — a drifting reading wanders a little around its level, while a fluctuating one climbs and drops by real amounts.
Lurch is stronger than fluctuate — fluctuating numbers rise and fall within some rough range, but lurching ones slam from level to level hard enough to alarm.

To waver is to move unsteadily or hesitate — a flame wavers, a voice wavers, a mind wavers over a decision. Fluctuate is the numerical cousin: readings and prices fluctuate, rising and falling irregularly by measurable amounts rather than trembling in place.

To seesaw is to tip back and forth between two states, one end going up at the very moment the other goes down. Fluctuate claims less: a fluctuating value simply rises and falls irregularly around some middle, with no paired trade-off and no second party involved.

To vary is simply to differ from time to time or case to case — the plainest word for change, with no picture in it. Fluctuate paints the picture: an up-and-down movement, irregular but continual, around some rough middle level.

The bakery's flour costs fluctuated all year, jumping after a poor harvest report, easing when imports arrived, and leaping again before the holidays, so the owner reprices her bread quarterly instead of chasing every move.
Fluctuate is for irregular rise and fall around some rough middle — no trend, no rhythm, just movement.
If the swings alternate between two poles on a beat, oscillate is the sharper word; if the numbers only sink, they are not fluctuating, they are falling.
Fluctuate is at home in reports and data — prices, temperatures, and readings fluctuate.
It promises irregularity, so do not use it for a steady climb or a clean rhythm: a metronome does not fluctuate.
Compare oscillate, which swings between two set poles, and vary, which claims nothing about the shape of the change.

The science fair project looked simple: measure the creek's depth every day for two months.
The readings refused to behave.
Monday's stick showed nine inches; Thursday's, fourteen; the following week the creek sat at eleven, then dipped to eight after a dry spell.
Her graph came out a jagged ribbon, climbing and falling with no rhythm she could name, yet never wandering far from about eleven inches.
Her conclusion embraced the mess: the creek's depth fluctuates — irregular in its rises and drops, but loyal to its middle.
The judges gave the honesty a ribbon of its own.
